name: Knee Osteoarthritis
summary: Clinical osteoarthritis causing activity-related knee pain, stiffness and functional limitation; exercise and education are core treatments.

redFlags: Hot swollen joint with systemic illness
Suspected infection, malignancy or inflammatory arthritis
firstSteps: Explain OA as manageable and not simply irreversible wear
selfCare: Weight-management support when appropriate and desired

assess: Weight, sleep and activity factors where relevant

tests.name: Clinical OA Pattern
tests.purpose: Recognize a typical clinical presentation without routine imaging.
tests.positive: Age ≥45, activity-related pain and no morning stiffness or stiffness ≤30 minutes, without atypical features.

tests.name: 30-Second Chair Stand
tests.positive: Not a diagnostic positive/negative test; lower performance indicates functional limitation and provides a baseline.

stages.label: Education & Symptom-Calibrated Activity
stages.goal: Improve understanding, confidence and tolerable daily activity.
do: Explain OA as manageable and not simply irreversible wear
dose: Aerobic work most days or accumulated through week as tolerated
moveOn: Improved daily activity and recovery from exercise

stages.label: Progressive Strength & Aerobic Fitness
when: Improved daily activity and recovery from exercise
do: Walking/cycling/aquatic aerobic exercise based on preference
dose: Aerobic: build toward regular moderate-duration sessions

stages.label: Long-Term Self-Management
do: Medical review if symptoms substantially impair quality of life despite appropriate nonsurgical care
dose: Maintain progressive strength 2–3 times/week plus regular aerobic activity

returnCriteria: OA is usually managed rather than 'cleared'; focus on meaningful walking, stairs, work/recreation and self-management goals.
Escalate for joint replacement opinion when pain/stiffness/function substantially affect quality of life and nonsurgical management is ineffective or unsuitable.

logic: Strength and physical activity are the core treatment. Pain does not automatically mean joint damage is worsening.
Choose exercise around the patient's functional goals: stairs, walking, sit-to-stand, prayer positions or community mobility.
Manual therapy is mainly used to make exercise and movement easier.
structures: Subchondral bone, cartilage, synovium and surrounding muscle/function
classification: Radiographic severity does not perfectly match symptoms
investigations: Do not routinely image a typical clinical OA presentation.
Use imaging when atypical features suggest another/additional diagnosis or when it will change management.
manual: For knee OA, manual therapy may be considered only alongside therapeutic exercise.
Use mobilization/soft-tissue work for selected mobility or pain goals, not as stand-alone treatment.
Tibiofemoral or patellofemoral mobilization for painful stiffness
MWM when it improves a functional movement
Patellar or tibiofemoral mobilization can be used when a clear mobility restriction is relevant.
Use Grade I–II for pain-dominant presentations and higher grades for safe stiffness-dominant restriction.
MWM can be trialed during squat/step if it immediately reduces pain.
modalities: NICE does not recommend routine TENS, therapeutic ultrasound, interferential, laser, pulsed short-wave or NMES for OA due to insufficient evidence of benefit.
Heat/cold may still be used pragmatically for comfort if safe, but should not replace core treatment.
Heat may help stiffness; cold may help post-activity soreness
TENS may offer short-term analgesia in selected patients
Ultrasound is not a core treatment
Heat: 10–15 minutes for stiffness if helpful.
Cold: 10–15 minutes after activity for symptom relief if preferred.
TENS can be an adjunct for short-term pain but should not replace strengthening.
dosing: Sit-to-stand or squat-to-chair: 2–3 sets × 6–12 reps, 2–4 days/week.
Knee extension or quadriceps strengthening: 2–4 sets × 6–15 reps, progressing resistance.
Aerobic walking/cycling: build toward 20–30 minutes most days if tolerated.
progression: Increase resistance and functional depth gradually
Progress from supported to loaded functional tasks
Increase resistance when the patient completes the top end of the rep range with good form and symptoms settle within about 24 hours.
Progress chair height, step height, walking distance and external load gradually.
Use function, not pain elimination, as the only progression target.
mistakes: Telling patients exercise damages the joint
Using imaging severity as the main treatment target
Avoiding strength training because of crepitus.
Not loading the quadriceps enough to create adaptation.
Progressing too fast after a long period of inactivity.
pearls: Some increase in pain when starting exercise can occur; consistent tailored exercise improves long-term pain and function.
Explain that radiographic changes and symptom severity do not always match; treatment should target function, goals and the person's lived symptoms.
Choose aerobic, strengthening and neuromuscular exercise according to capability and preference, then progress gradually and consistently.
A temporary manageable symptom response can be acceptable, but sustained flare, new swelling or unexpected deterioration warrants dose review and reassessment.
Weight-management conversations, when relevant, should be respectful, collaborative and focused on support rather than blame.
education: Explain that exercise is safe and can improve pain/function even when X-rays show OA.
Discuss body-weight management sensitively only when relevant and desired.
escalation: Medical review for persistent severe disability, recurrent large effusions or consideration of injection/surgical options

tests.name: Clinical OA Pattern
tests.purpose: Recognize a typical clinical presentation without routine imaging.
tests.positive: Age ≥45, activity-related pain and no morning stiffness or stiffness ≤30 minutes, without atypical features.
tests.patientPosition: History plus standing, walking and functional examination.
tests.handPlacement: As needed for palpation and ROM.
procedure: Assess ROM, strength, gait and function.
tests.interpretation: NICE supports a clinical diagnosis of OA without routine imaging in this typical pattern.

tests.name: 30-Second Chair Stand
tests.positive: Not a diagnostic positive/negative test; lower performance indicates functional limitation and provides a baseline.
tests.patientPosition: Sitting in a standard chair, arms folded if safe.
procedure: On 'go', stand fully and sit repeatedly for 30 seconds.
Count completed stands with consistent technique.
tests.interpretation: Useful outcome measure for progression, not proof of OA.

story.headline: The knee with a soundtrack—and a future beyond the X-ray
story.scene: A 59-year-old teacher walks upstairs with a crunch and declares, 'My knee sounds like a packet of chips. I'm finished.' She has reduced her walks because of a scan report.
story.dialogue: Patient: 'Does this mean I must stop exercising?' Therapist: 'Your knee hasn't sent a retirement letter. We just need a smarter training plan.'
story.clue: Activity-related pain, stiffness and gradual function change can fit OA, but imaging severity and pain do not align perfectly. Screen a hot, acutely swollen joint or systemic illness.
story.twist: Exercise may cause temporary, tolerable symptoms at the start. That does not automatically mean joint damage is progressing.
story.aha: A noisy knee is not a prediction of disability.
story.patientTranslation: Osteoarthritis is a common joint condition, and many people improve their daily function with strength training, activity adjustments and support. A scan doesn't dictate everything your knee can do.
story.clinicianReasoning: Assess function, stiffness pattern, swelling, comorbidities and red flags. Educate on activity and weight management where relevant, prescribe individualized strength and aerobic exercise, monitor symptom response.
story.rehabBridge: Start with manageable walking and sit-to-stand → build lower-limb strength and aerobic capacity → practice stairs and meaningful daily tasks.
story.question: A person with uncomplicated knee OA fears that strengthening will wear the knee out. Best response?
options: Offer tailored progressive exercise and education
Use X-ray severity as the sole determinant of ability
story.explanation: Guideline-supported core OA care includes exercise and education; the plan should be individualized and symptoms monitored.
